parsed_response.case_orientation: This Supreme Court of Canada decision addresses whether, under s. 34(1)(e) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), a finding of inadmissibility for 'engaging in acts of violence that would or might endanger the lives or safety of persons in Canada' requires a nexus to national security or the security of Canada. The case arises from judicial review of administrative decisions (Immigration Appeal Division and Immigration Division) that interpreted s. 34(1)(e) as not requiring such a nexus. The Federal Court allowed judicial review, but the Federal Court of Appeal reversed, upholding the administrative interpretation. The Supreme Court (majority, per Jamal J.) holds that reasonableness is the standard of review, that the administrative decisions were unreasonable, and that s. 34(1)(e) requires a nexus to national security or the security of Canada. Côté J. concurs in the result but would apply correctness review to certified questions. (Evidence: paras 1–12, 34–54, 121–123, 124–127, 189; citation_ids: 7658399, 7658403, 7658405, 7658407, 7658413, 7658414, 7658415, 7658511, 7658512, 7658513, 7658514, 7658515, 7658516, 7658517, 7658518, 7658519, 7658520, 7658521, 7658522, 7658523, 7658524, 7658525, 7658526, 7658527, 7658528, 7658529, 7658530, 7658531, 7658532, 7658533, 7658534, 7658535, 7658536, 7658537, 7658538, 7658539).

core_propositions: The case concerns the interpretation of s. 34(1)(e) IRPA and the standard of review for administrative decisions involving statutory interpretation in immigration law.
The Supreme Court applies the Vavilov framework, holding that reasonableness is the presumptive standard of review unless an exception applies.
No established exception to reasonableness review applies to certified questions under s. 74(d) IRPA.
The administrative decisions were unreasonable for failing to address key statutory context, consequences, and international law constraints.
The only reasonable interpretation of s. 34(1)(e) requires a nexus to national security or the security of Canada.
citation_treatment_patterns: Vavilov is applied as binding authority for the standard of review framework.
Pushpanathan and pre-Vavilov cases are discussed and distinguished.
International law (Refugee Convention) is treated as a binding interpretive constraint.

argument_map.proposition: The standard of review for administrative decisions interpreting s. 34(1)(e) IRPA is reasonableness, not correctness, even where a certified question is present.
argument_map.legal_issue: Standard of review for certified questions under IRPA
argument_map.response: Côté J. (concurring) argues for correctness review for certified questions.

argument_map.proposition: The administrative decisions were unreasonable because they failed to address key statutory context, the broad consequences of their interpretation, and international law constraints (non-refoulement).
argument_map.legal_issue: Reasonableness of administrative interpretation of s. 34(1)(e)

authorities_used.role: recent SCC authority on international law constraints

argument_map.response: No material counter-argument from the dissent; Côté J. agrees the decisions were unreasonable.

argument_map.proposition: The only reasonable interpretation of s. 34(1)(e) IRPA is that it requires a nexus to national security or the security of Canada.
argument_map.response: Côté J. concurs in this interpretation.

argument_map.proposition: Certified questions under s. 74(d) IRPA should be reviewed for correctness, not reasonableness, due to legislative intent and the rule of law.
argument_map.legal_issue: Standard of review for certified questions under IRPA
argument_map.response: Majority rejects this, holding reasonableness is the standard.

citation_treatment.normalized_citation: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, [2019] 4 S.C.R. 653
citation_treatment.argument_role: binding precedent for standard of review
citation_treatment.authority_proposition: Establishes the presumptive standard of reasonableness for judicial review of administrative decisions, subject to limited exceptions.
citation_treatment.treatment_explanation: The majority applies Vavilov as the controlling authority for the standard of review framework, directly following its methodology and exceptions. (paras 7, 9, 39, 51, 54, 56–66, 121–122)

evidence.source_quote: In Vavilov, this Court established a presumption that when a court reviews the merits of an administrative decision, the standard of review is reasonableness. This presumption is rebutted in two types of situations...

citation_treatment.proposition_in_this_case: Reasonableness is the standard of review for administrative decisions interpreting s. 34(1)(e) IRPA.

citation_treatment.normalized_citation: Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1998] 1 S.C.R. 982
citation_treatment.argument_role: pre-Vavilov authority for correctness on certified questions
citation_treatment.authority_proposition: Certified questions of general importance under the Immigration Act should be reviewed for correctness.
citation_treatment.treatment_explanation: The majority distinguishes Pushpanathan as pre-Vavilov and not controlling post-Vavilov, while Côté J. relies on it to support correctness review. (paras 37, 126, 128, 129, 132)

evidence.source_quote: Citing pre-Vavilov jurisprudence, they say that because the appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal involved a 'serious question of general importance' certified under s. 74(d) of the IRPA, it would be 'incoherent' if the standard were not correctness (A.F., at para. 49, citing Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1998] 1 S.C.R. 982, at para. 43).

citation_treatment.proposition_in_this_case: Côté J. argues for correctness review based on Pushpanathan.

citation_treatment.normalized_citation: Canadian Council for Refugees v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 SCC 17, at paras. 43-48
citation_treatment.argument_role: recent SCC authority on international law constraints
citation_treatment.authority_proposition: International law, including the Refugee Convention, is a binding interpretive constraint on IRPA.
citation_treatment.treatment_explanation: The majority uses Canadian Council for Refugees to reinforce that international law (non-refoulement) must be considered in interpreting s. 34(1)(e). (paras 104–117)

evidence.source_quote: The IAD failed to interpret and apply s. 34(1)(e) in compliance with international human rights instruments to which Canada is a signatory — specifically, the obligation of non-refoulement under Article 33(1) of the 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, contrary to the express direction in s. 3(3)(f) of the IRPA that it must do so.

citation_treatment.proposition_in_this_case: International law is a binding constraint on the interpretation of s. 34(1)(e).

statute_and_issue_intelligence.provision: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 34(1)(e)
statute_and_issue_intelligence.issue_or_argument: Whether s. 34(1)(e) requires a nexus to national security or the security of Canada for a finding of inadmissibility.

statute_and_issue_intelligence.provision: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 74(d)
statute_and_issue_intelligence.issue_or_argument: Whether the presence of a certified question under s. 74(d) changes the standard of review from reasonableness to correctness.

statute_and_issue_intelligence.provision: Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, Article 33(1)
statute_and_issue_intelligence.issue_or_argument: Whether the administrative interpretation of s. 34(1)(e) is consistent with Canada's non-refoulement obligations.

unresolved_questions: Whether, in future cases, the Supreme Court will recognize a new correctness category for certified questions outside the IRPA context remains unresolved.

The precise boundaries of what constitutes a 'nexus to national security or the security of Canada' under s. 34(1)(e) are not defined in this decision and are left to future administrative application.

unsupported_or_ambiguous_findings: The decision does not define the precise threshold for 'nexus to national security or the security of Canada' under s. 34(1)(e).
The record does not resolve whether the Supreme Court would extend correctness review to certified questions in other statutory contexts.
